10. Date of final order : 05.06.2025 1.
The accused is facing trial for offence u/s 420/468/471 IPC.

The genesis of the prosecution story is that in the year 2009 at unknown time at PHQ, Delhi within the jurisdiction of PS IP Estate accused submitted form no. 1218 with forged DL No. 15851/MTR/03 issued from Transport Authority, Mathura, UP for the post of driver in Delhi Police and fraudulently and dishonestly induced the examining / appointing authority of Delhi Police to believe that the same was original /
genuine and on accused's representation, he was provisionally selected for the post of driver (Constable) in Delhi Police and also on the abovesaid date, time and place he used the forged DL No.
15851/MTR/03 as genuine which he knew or had reason to believe that the same was forged and thus committed an offence u/s 420/468/471 IPC.
Pursuant to the complaint made by the complainant, the criminal law was set into motion vide registration of the FIR against accused.
The aforesaid person was however, never arrested by the police.

On completion of investigation, the State vs Kuldeep Kumar on 5 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/96396326/

5. After prosecution evidence and defence evidence, the statement of accused u/s 313 Cr.P.C. was recorded, wherein all the incriminating circumstances were offered to accused.
Thereafter, accused led evidence in his defence.
6. In order to support his case, accused examined two witnesses in his defence.

In brief, the testimonies of defence witnesses are discussed as under:
6.1 DW-1 Kuldeep Kumar deposed that he was the accused in the present matter.
In the year 2009, the vacancies for the Ct. Male (driver) in Delhi Police were published.

When he was waiting for his joining and training letter in the meanwhile instead, he received a show Cause notice from Sh. Ishwar Singh, the then Deputy Commissioner of Police,

6.2 DW-2 Ravi Karan Singh deposed that he was posted at the office of ARTO Mathura from 2005 till 2016, as Junior Assistant and was specifically posted at check post.
He was transferred from ARTO Mathura in the year 2016 and was again transferred to the said office.
After that he was transferred to ARTO Kasganj in the year 2022.

The ARTO office Mathura, had received a request for verification of 201 driving licenses from the office of Deputy Commissioner of Police, Provisions and Logistics vide letter number 1193/East P & L/Delhi, dated 01.02.2010.
In pursuance of which the record keeper posted at the said authority prepared the verification reports while tallying the licenses under scrutiny with the records preserved.
The conclusive verification report was handed over by him to ASI Devenderpal Singh on the 16/03/2010 vide letter number 255/License/Satyapan/2010 dated 03/03/2010.
The said verification report contained 201 proforma individually.

The witness was cross-examined by Ld. APP for the state.

5 7.

I have heard the contentions advanced by Ld. APP for the State and also by Ld.
Defence counsel representing the accused.

8. Ld. APP for State has contended that the prosecution has proved its case beyond all reasonable doubts and therefore, the accused is liable to be convicted for offence u/s 420/511 and 471 IPC.
9.
Per contra, Ld.
Defence counsel for accused has vehemently argued that the prosecution has failed to establish guilt of accused beyond all reasonable doubts.
It is argued that the verification report on the basis of which prosecution was initiated against accused has not been proved as the author of the reports have not deposed.
He further argued that the original record from ARTO office could not made available.
He further argued that the verification report pertaining to year 2018 could not have been prepared on the basis of original records as admittedly the original record was destroyed in year 2016.
With these submissions, prayer is made for acquittal of accused persons from the alleged offences.

10. Having discussed the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses, the following issues emerge for our consideration:-
1.
Whether the action of accused constitute the offence of cheating u/s 420 IPC.
2. Whether accused forged the driving license punishable u/s 471 IPC.

Analysis:
The Hon'ble Supereme Court of India in Mariam Fasihuddin & Anr. Vs. State by Adugodi Police Station & Anr. Crl. Apeal no. 335/2024 observed The offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC:
10. Section 420 IPC provides that whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy, the whole or any part of valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be liable to be punished for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.

entities.text: Mariam Fasihuddin & Anr. Vs. State by Adugodi Police Station & Anr. Crl. Apeal no. 335/2024
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Further, Section 415 IPC distinctly defines the term'cheating'.

The provision elucidates that an act marked by fraudulent or dishonest intentions will be categorised as 'cheating' if it is intended to induce the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, causing damage or harm to that person.
State vs Kuldeep Kumar on 5 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/96396326/
6 11.It

is thus paramount that in order to attract the provisions of Section 420 IPC, the prosecution has to not only prove that the accused has cheated someone but also that by doing so, he has dishonestly induced the person who is cheated to deliver property.

There are, thus, three components of this offence, i.e., (I) the deception 10 P a g e of any person, (ii)
fraudulently or dishonestly inducing that person to deliver any property to any person, and (iii)
mensrea or dishonest intention of the accused at the time of making the inducement.
There is no gainsaid that for the offence of cheating, fraudulent and dishonest intention must exist from the inception when the promise or representation was made.
12.It is well known that every deceitful act is not unlawful, just as not every unlawful act is deceitful.
Some acts may be termed both as unlawful as well as deceitful, and such acts alone will fall within the purview of Section 420 IPC.

It must also be understood that a statement of fact is deemed 'deceitful' when it is false, and is knowingly or recklessly made with the intent that it shall be acted upon by another person, resulting in damage or loss.2 'Cheating' therefore, generally involves a preceding deceitful act that dishonestly induces a person to deliver any property or any part of a valuable security, prompting the induced person to undertake the said act, which they would not have done but for the inducement.
13.Theterm 'property' employed in Section 420 IPC has a well defined connotation.
Every species of valuable right or interest that is subject to ownership and has an exchangeable value-is ordinarily understood as 'property'.
It also describes one's exclusive right to possess, use and dispose of a thing.

The IPC itself defines the term 2 P. Ramanatha Aiyar, Advanced Law Lexicon, 6th Edition, Vol. 1,
pg.903.
11| P a g e 'moveable property' as, "intended to include corporeal property of every description,
except land and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth."
Whereas immoveable property is generally understood to mean land, benefits arising out of land and things attached or permanently fastened to the earth.

The offence of forgery under Sections 468 and 471 IPC: 21.The offence of 'forgery' under Section 468 IPC postulates that whoever commits forgery, intending that the document or electronic document forged, shall be used for the purpose of cheating, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Whereas Section 471 IPC states that whoever fraudulently or dishonestly uses as genuine any documents which he knows or has reason to believe it 15 | P a g e to be a forged document, shall be punished in the same manner as if he had forged such document.

22.There are two primary components that need to be fulfilled in order to establish the offence of 'forgery', namely: (I) that the accused has fabricated an instrument; and (ii) it was done with the intention that the forged document would be used for the purpose of cheating.

Simply put, the State vs Kuldeep Kumar on 5 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/96396326/
7 offence of forgery requires the preparation of a false document with the dishonest intention of causing damage or injury.
23.The
offences of 'forgery' and 'cheating' intersect and converge, as the act of forgery is committed with the intent to deceive or cheat an individual.
Having extensively addressed the aspect of dishonest intent in the context of 'cheating' under Section 420 IPC, it stands established that no dishonest intent can be made out against the Appellants.

Our focus therefore will now be confined,
for the sake of brevity, to the first element, i.e.,the preparation of a false document.
The determination of whether the Appellants prepared a false document, by forging Respondent No. 2's signature, however, cannot be even prima facie ascertained at this juncture.
Considering the primary ingredient of dishonest intention itself could not be established against the Appellants, the offence of forgery too, has no legs to stand.
It is also significant to highlight that the proceedings as against the concerned Passport Officer, who was implicated as Accused No. 4, already stand quashed.
In such like situation and coupled with the nature of allegations, we are unable to appreciate as to why the Appellants be subjected to the ordeal of trial.

11. The case of prosecution as per original complaint Ex. PW5/A is that accused applied for the vacancies of Constable(driver) upon the strength of the heavy driving license no. 15851/MTR/03 issued from ARTO Mathura on 17.11.2003 having its validity upto 11.05.2009 but upon the verification, the DL was not found issued and found not valid upon the basis of letter no.
619/DL/verification/2011 dated 11.08.2011.
In the trial, PW-5 complainant proved the original complaint Ex. PW5/A by identifying his signatures upon the complaint and affirming the version of complaint.
12. During the trial, the prosecution was required to prove all the verification reports on the basis of which the charge-sheet was filed against accused.

The original verification report no.
619/DL/verification/2011 dated 11.08.2011 has not been exhibited by the prosecution in the trial.
Even the author who prepared the aforestated verification report has not been examined by the prosecution.

There is another verification report issued during the investigation having no.
1883/licence satyapan/2018 dated 09.05.2018 Ex. PW7/B.
This report remarks that the license bearing no. 15851/MTR/03 was not issued.
It is further remarked that the aforestated license was found to be fake.
The prosecution was required to prove that both the verification reports were prepared from the original record available in the ATRO Office, Mathura.
However, Ld. Predecessor examined Sh. Pradeep Kumar Singh, the then ARTO, Mathura as Court witness as the original record was not made available during the trial.

13. Sh. Pradeep Kumar Singh, Court witness deposed that due to one fire incident on 16.05.2016, the record lying in the record room was gutted in fire for which GD no. 64 dated 18.05.2016 was registered.
He further deposed that the required original DL verification reports were not available in the ARTO, Office and cannot be produced as the records and reports were destroyed in fire.
However, he could not bring anything on record showing that the record pertaining to the present matter was also destroyed.
No punchnama or seizure memo has been placed on record by the then ARTO Mathura to show that the record pertaining to the present matter was destroyed.

Merely placing on record one photocopy of GD No. 64 dated 18.05.2016 is not sufficient to discharge the State vs Kuldeep Kumar on 5 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/96396326/
8 burden of ARTO, Mathura from bringing the original record.
14. Section 65(c) of Indian Evidence Act allows the admissibility of secondary evidence in the case when the original has been destroyed or lost or when the party offering evidence of its contents cannot, for any other reason not arising from his own record or neglect, produce it in reasonable time but in the present case, ARTO, Mathura has failed to satisfy that the original record could not be made available for reasons not beyond their control.
Merely saying that one fire incident caused destruction of the record does not absolve the liability of prosecution from bringing originals on record.

Even otherwise, prosecution could have brought certified copies of the record as the record sought by this Court was public record but even the certified copies of the record have not been brought on record.
15.
Coming further, there is another verification report Ex. PW7/B issued in year 2018.
When the original record was already destroyed in year 2016, the verification report could not have been prepared after tallying from the original record.

However, it has been clarified by the Court witness,
Sh. Pradeep Kumar Singh, the then ARTO, Mathura that the replies were sent on the basis of photocopies of DL verification reports available in ARTO office, Mathura.

Even otherwise, Ex.
PW7/B states that the license bearing no. 15851/MTR/03 was not issued.

The verification report was prepared by Ms. Babita Verma, the then ARTO Official and the report was attested by Md.
Ibrahim, the then Senior Assistant, ARTO Official.
Ms. Babita was not cited as witness in the list of witnesses.

PW-8 Md. Ibrahim was examined by prosecution to prove the report bearing no.
1883/licence / satyapan/20118 dated 09.05.2018 Ex. PW7/B.

However, in his cross-examination, he deposed that he had merely countersigned the letter Ex. PW7/B at the instance of Ms. Babita Verma,
the then ARTO Official who prepared the report under her signature.

He further admitted in his cross-examination that he did not know whether any document was annexed with the report Ex.
PW7/B.
He further admitted that the Ex. PW7/B is not descriptive.
He further deposed that he had checked the cash book prior to signing of report Ex. PW7/B.

However, the Court witness Sh.
Pradeep Kumar Singh, the then ARTO Official deposed that the original record was not available.
When original record was not available, it is beyond comprehension as to how PW-8 Md. Ibrahim could check the cash book register before signing the report.

The trial record is reflective of the fact that Ld. Predecessor issued several notices to ARTO Mathura to bring the record but the record could not be brought and therefore, ordersheet dated 07.07.2023, reflects that same and the Ld.
Predecessor was constrained to examine Sh. Pradeep Kumar Singh, the then ARTO as Court witness.
16.
The moot question is when the original record was not available with ARTO Mathura in year 2018, how could letter Ex. PW7/B be prepared.
It cannot be ignored that PW-7 IO SI Sandeep Singh issued notice u/s 91 Cr.PC to DTO, Mathura seeking the required information.

The notice u/s 91 Cr.PC is Ex.PW7/A and IO sought the information such as the name of MLO on the date of issuance of license, submission of requisite fees by accused and so on but ARTO Official replied to the notice in only one line with remarks " jari nahi hai".
The other queries posed by IO Ex. PW7/A were not addressed at all by ARTO official for reason best known to them.
More surprisingly, PW-7 IO SI Sandeep Singh did not take any other action against the officials of ARTO Mathura for not providing the information which was repeatedly sought by the IO.

PW-7 SI Sandeep Singh admitted that he State vs Kuldeep Kumar on 5 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/96396326/
9 did not interrogate any officials of ARTO, Mathura and he only served the notice u/s 91 Cr.PC.
There is no explanation as to why the ARTO officials were not interrogated even when they did not reply to the notice issued by IO in detail.
Coming further Ex.
PW7/E is the extract of DL issued from ARTO Baghpat as per which the license was renewed / endorsed by Baghpat Authority on the basis of issuance of DL from Mathura Authority, UP.
Even, PW7 SI Sandeep Singh admitted in his cross- examination that the positive report was received from ARTO Baghpat that the DL of accused was genuine for driving HM vehicle.
17. Another aspect to be considered is that the report dated 11.08.2011 also reflects that the license was not issued but the signatory of the report has not been examined by the prosecution.

Examination of author of the report dated 11.08.2011 could have been beneficial for the prosecution but the IO did not even mention the name of the person who signed on original report dated 11.08.2011, upon the basis of which FIR was registered.

18. Furthermore, during the trial, Ld. Predecessor vide order dated 07.07.2023 examined court witness Sh. Pradeep Kumar Singh, the then ARTO Mathura who deposed that the original verification reports were not available as the verification report were gutted in the fire.

The photocopies of the verification reports would have been considered by this court as per the section 65(c) of the Indian Evidence Act if prosecution would have shown that the verification report pertaining to the present matter was gutted in fire or brought the author of these reports as per section 67 of the Indian Evidence Act but as discussed in the preceding paras, the authors of the reports were not examined either.

19. Coming to the defence placed by accused, it is observed that he examined himself as DW-1 stating that as per one verification report mark DW1/A the DL number was found to be issued in the name of accused.
Though mark DW1/A is a reply received by way of RTI but mark DW1/A does not specify that the license bearing no. 15851/MTR/03 was found issued in name of accused.
Ld. APP cross- examined DW-1 on the aspect how accused being permanent resident of Sonipat got issued one DL from ARTO Mathura.
DW-1 deposed in his cross-examination that he resided in Mathura from year 2003 to year 2004 as he was working as tourist guide at that time.

However, there is nothing on record to substantiate that accused was actually working as tourist guide in Mathura at the relevant period of time except for one affidavit verified by the IO stating that he was residing in Mathura.
Even this document is a self serving document.

The admission of accused that he applied for the DL in Mathura and not in Sonipat, Haryana as he had attained the majority age for issuance of DL in Haryana casts doubt upon the averment that accused was actually residing in Mathura.
20. However, it is the settled law that it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the case beyond reasonable doubts, the burden of proof can never be shifted to the defence.

In the present matter,
prosecution had to prove that accused with dishonest intention got the forged DL issued in his favour and tried to cause wrongful loss to the complainant but as discussed in the previous paras,
prosecution could not prove that the DL no. 15851/MTR/03 was not issued in the name of accused and accused had knowledge that DL No. 15851/MTR/03 was genuine and despite knowing, he used the DL while applying for the vacancies.
The authors of the verification reports never deposed before the court.
The alleged forged DL was never sent to FSL to show that it was fraudulently prepared.

State vs Kuldeep Kumar on 5 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/96396326/
10 21.

As an outcome of the discussion made above, this Court is of the view that the answers to the issues framed at S.No. 1 and 2 are in negative and prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubts and benefit of doubt must be given to the accused.

Accordingly, accused Kuldeep Kumar is acquitted for offences u/s 420/511/471 IPC.

opennyai_summary.issue: Whether the action of accused constitute the offence of cheating u/s 420 IPC.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Analysis:
The Hon'ble Supereme Court of India in Mariam Fasihuddin & Anr. Vs. State by Adugodi Police Station & Anr. Crl. Apeal no. 335/2024 observed The offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC:
10. Section 420 IPC provides that whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy, the whole or any part of valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be liable to be punished for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.
is thus paramount that in order to attract the provisions of Section 420 IPC, the prosecution has to not only prove that the accused has cheated someone but also that by doing so, he has dishonestly induced the person who is cheated to deliver property.
There are, thus, three components of this offence, i.e., (I) the deception 10 P a g e of any person, (ii)
fraudulently or dishonestly inducing that person to deliver any property to any person, and (iii)
mensrea or dishonest intention of the accused at the time of making the inducement.
There is no gainsaid that for the offence of cheating, fraudulent and dishonest intention must exist from the inception when the promise or representation was made.
12.It is well known that every deceitful act is not unlawful, just as not every unlawful act is deceitful.
Some acts may be termed both as unlawful as well as deceitful, and such acts alone will fall within the purview of Section 420 IPC.
It must also be understood that a statement of fact is deemed 'deceitful' when it is false, and is knowingly or recklessly made with the intent that it shall be acted upon by another person, resulting in damage or loss.2 'Cheating' therefore, generally involves a preceding deceitful act that dishonestly induces a person to deliver any property or any part of a valuable security, prompting the induced person to undertake the said act, which they would not have done but for the inducement.
offences of 'forgery' and 'cheating' intersect and converge, as the act of forgery is committed with the intent to deceive or cheat an individual.
Having extensively addressed the aspect of dishonest intent in the context of 'cheating' under Section 420 IPC, it stands established that no dishonest intent can be made out against the Appellants.
Our focus therefore will now be confined,
for the sake of brevity, to the first element, i.e.,the preparation of a false document.
The determination of whether the Appellants prepared a false document, by forging Respondent No. 2's signature, however, cannot be even prima facie ascertained at this juncture.
Considering the primary ingredient of dishonest intention itself could not be established against the Appellants, the offence of forgery too, has no legs to stand.
In such like situation and coupled with the nature of allegations, we are unable to appreciate as to why the Appellants be subjected to the ordeal of trial.
11. The case of prosecution as per original complaint Ex. PW5/A is that accused applied for the vacancies of Constable(driver) upon the strength of the heavy driving license no. 15851/MTR/03 issued from ARTO Mathura on 17.11.2003 having its validity upto 11.05.2009 but upon the verification, the DL was not found issued and found not valid upon the basis of letter no.
619/DL/verification/2011 dated 11.08.2011.
In the trial, PW-5 complainant proved the original complaint Ex. PW5/A by identifying his signatures upon the complaint and affirming the version of complaint.
12. During the trial, the prosecution was required to prove all the verification reports on the basis of which the charge-sheet was filed against accused.
Merely placing on record one photocopy of GD No. 64 dated 18.05.2016 is not sufficient to discharge the State vs Kuldeep Kumar on 5 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/96396326/
8 burden of ARTO, Mathura from bringing the original record.
14. Section 65(c) of Indian Evidence Act allows the admissibility of secondary evidence in the case when the original has been destroyed or lost or when the party offering evidence of its contents cannot, for any other reason not arising from his own record or neglect, produce it in reasonable time but in the present case, ARTO, Mathura has failed to satisfy that the original record could not be made available for reasons not beyond their control.
Merely saying that one fire incident caused destruction of the record does not absolve the liability of prosecution from bringing originals on record.
Even otherwise, prosecution could have brought certified copies of the record as the record sought by this Court was public record but even the certified copies of the record have not been brought on record.
15.
Examination of author of the report dated 11.08.2011 could have been beneficial for the prosecution but the IO did not even mention the name of the person who signed on original report dated 11.08.2011, upon the basis of which FIR was registered.
The photocopies of the verification reports would have been considered by this court as per the section 65(c) of the Indian Evidence Act if prosecution would have shown that the verification report pertaining to the present matter was gutted in fire or brought the author of these reports as per section 67 of the Indian Evidence Act but as discussed in the preceding paras, the authors of the reports were not examined either.
However, there is nothing on record to substantiate that accused was actually working as tourist guide in Mathura at the relevant period of time except for one affidavit verified by the IO stating that he was residing in Mathura.
Even this document is a self serving document.
The admission of accused that he applied for the DL in Mathura and not in Sonipat, Haryana as he had attained the majority age for issuance of DL in Haryana casts doubt upon the averment that accused was actually residing in Mathura.
20. However, it is the settled law that it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the case beyond reasonable doubts, the burden of proof can never be shifted to the defence.
In the present matter,
prosecution had to prove that accused with dishonest intention got the forged DL issued in his favour and tried to cause wrongful loss to the complainant but as discussed in the previous paras,
prosecution could not prove that the DL no. 15851/MTR/03 was not issued in the name of accused and accused had knowledge that DL No. 15851/MTR/03 was genuine and despite knowing, he used the DL while applying for the vacancies.
The authors of the verification reports never deposed before the court.
The alleged forged DL was never sent to FSL to show that it was fraudulently prepared.
